The many varieties of the gramas, murchhanas and talas
are not stated, since they are of no use for the present subject and are unknowable.

This is said in the section on talas:
These talas are five thousand and thirty-three.

Having praised Shiva with the agnishtomika tala, one becomes auspicious.
Here the pure talas have names — Agnishtoma and the rest —*
notes: The Agnishtoma is a Vedic soma sacrifice; in the treatises on music the pure tanas bear the names of Vedic sacrifices. "Becomes auspicious" is śivo bhavet, a play on words: after praising Shiva one "becomes shiva (auspicious)."

verses_en.text: but, owing to their unfitness for practice, I have not listed them.*
notes: So in A (by the scan: «সন্তি প্রয়োগবৈধুর্য্যান্ন ময়া তাঃ প্রকীর্ত্তিতাঃ»; prayoga-vaidhuryān na, "owing to unfitness for practice — not"); the 1960 edition has vaidhuryāya, C vaidhuryām.

verses_en.text:
The good fortune of these talas is immense:
taking embodied form, they sport before Krishna.

Lalita and the other sakhis of Radhika, the group leaders (yutheshvaris),
each separately set the talas in motion.

Rai and Kanu, in supreme bliss, together with the sakhis
reveal varna and song in wondrous arrangements.*
notes: Varna is the character of melodic movement: sthayi, arohi, avarohi and sanchari (see 2659–2665).

verses_en.text:
Now varna is described.
The svara employed at the beginning of the act of singing is varna;
it is of four kinds, by which the singer is gladdened.

Sthayi varna, the arohi and avarohi varnas, and also
sanchari — the characteristics of these four are proclaimed.

When one and the same svara is used with pauses again and again,
it is sthayi varna — so it is acknowledged in all views.

The arohi and avarohi svaras [after] sthayi are according to the sense [of their names];
the varna in which these three are mixed is accepted as sanchari.*
notes: Sthāyy-anugatārtha: so in A (by the scan: «স্থায্যনুগতার্থ»), B, C; understood after the verse 2664: the names arohi ("ascending") and avarohi ("descending") speak for themselves.

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said]:
The svara employed at the beginning of the act of singing is called varna;
it is of four kinds: sthayi, arohi, avarohi and sanchari.

The definition of each:
If one and the same svara is used with pauses again and again,
that is to be known as sthayi varna; the other two have names according to their sense.
The other two are the arohi svara and the avarohi svara; they "have names according to their sense," that is, their names follow their meaning: the sense is — "arohi" in the meaning "it ascends," "avarohi" — "it descends."

In the Sangita-parijata:
If the use is with pauses again and again on each single svara,
that is to be known as sthayi varna; the other two have names according to their sense;
the varna [arising] from their mixture is called sanchari.
"Their" — [that is,] of the sthayi, arohi and avarohi svaras.

Sa-ri-ga-ma-pa-dha-ni — these varnas are the seven svaras;
by particular arrangements [of them there arise] a great many alankaras.*
notes: Alankara (lit. "ornament") is a melodic figure, an ordered combination of svaras; below (2674–2693) examples are given for each kind of varna.

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said]:
The varnas become alankaras through the particularities of arrangement.

The sthayi are twenty-six, the arohi certainly twelve,
the avarohi twelve, the sanchari twelve.

All together there are sixty-two kinds of alankaras;
among them are many varieties — [this] is proclaimed in the shastras.

Thus [it is said]:
The sthayi are twenty-six, the arohi twelve,
the sanchari twelve and the avarohi twelve.
Thus the sixty-two well-known alankaras are proclaimed.

The purposes of alankara are many:
the shastras name the strengthening of practice in the knowledge of the svaras and so on.

Thus [it is said]:
Firm practice in the knowledge of the svaras and the attainment of delight arise;
variety in the knowledge of the varnas — [such is] the purpose of alankara.

In the Sangita-parijata:
Without alankaras the ragas do not attain expansion.

On sthayi varna.
The guidance on the alankaras of sthayi varna is given thus:
the varna on which [the figure] begins comes again at the end.

Here I explain the alankara named Bhadra:
its arrangement is an order in which one svara at a time is dropped.

Thus [it is said] in the Parijata:
Where, beginning [from a svara] and going on to the next, one again utters the previous svara —
that alankara the wise Anjaneya called Bhadra.
Here the order [is formed] by dropping one svara at a time.
Example: sa-ri-sa, ri-ga-ri, ga-ma-ga, ma-pa-ma, pa-dha-pa, dha-ni-dha, ni-sa-ni, sa-ri-sa.

On arohi varna.
Thus I point the way in the arohi alankaras:
[the alankara] named Vistirna has long varnas on the seven svaras.

In the Parijata:
Where from the initial svara of the murchhana there is ascent in order
with long svaras, pausing on each, that [alankara] is called Vistirna.
Example: sā rī gā mā pā dhā nī.

The first two [svaras] short, the third syllable long —
[this] is the charming alankara named Prachchhadana.

In the Parijata:
Making the first two short and making the third long —
[this] the all-knowing Hanuman calls the excellent Sandhi-prachchhadana.*
Example: sa-ri-gā, ri-ga-mā, ga-ma-pā, ma-pa-dhā, pa-dha-nī, dha-ni-sā.
notes: The couplet 2679 has "Prachchhadana"; the verse has sandhi-pracchādana (A, B, C sandhiḥ pracchādanam).

verses_en.text:
[The alankara] named Udvahita: the first [svara] is uttered four times,
the second twice, the third and fourth once each.

In the Parijata:
The first svara four times, the second twice;
uttering the third once and likewise the fourth once —
[this] is the alankara Udvahita, proclaimed by Hanuman.*
Example: sa-sa-sa-sa ri-ri ga ma, ri-ri-ri-ri ga-ga ma pa, ga-ga-ga-ga ma-ma pa dha, ma-ma-ma-ma pa-pa dha ni, pa-pa-pa-pa dha-dha ni sa.
notes: A (by the scan: «আদ্যং স্বরং চতুর্ব্বারং দ্বিবারঞ্চ তৃতীয়কং») and B read dvivāraṃ ca tṛtīyakam ("the third twice"); the 1960 edition has ādyaṃ svaraṃ dvivāraṃ ca caturvāraṃ dvitīyakam ("the first twice, the second four times"). Translated according to the sense of the couplet 2681 and the example.

verses_en.text:
On avarohi varna.
The avarohi alankaras are of the same kind;
to speak [of them] is superfluous — others too do not speak of them.

In the Parijata:
These [same], in descending order, are the twelve avarohi;
because of the prolixity I have not written out the descent.

On sanchari varna.
It moves everywhere — therefore it [is called] sanchari;
I point the way, by which the singer has joy.

The first two varnas are repeated three times; after that
the third varna, and after it the second syllable.

Thus is described the alankara named Prasada;
in knowing all this there is joy — [so] it is proclaimed in the shastras.

In the Parijata:
And since they move about everywhere, therefore [they are] sanchari.

Repeating the first pair three times and uttering the third and [then] the second,
the wise have called that alankara Prasada.
Example: sa-ri sa-ri sa-ri ga-ri, ri-ga ri-ga ri-ga ma-ga, ga-ma ga-ma ga-ma pa-ma, ma-pa ma-pa ma-pa dha-pa, pa-dha pa-dha pa-dha ni-dha, dha-ni dha-ni dha-ni sa-ni.

Here there is one alankara named Akshepa:
three svaras are uttered in order, beginning from the first.

In the Parijata:
Where three svaras [go] in order, that the wise have called Akshepaka.
Example: sa-ri-ga, ri-ga-ma, ga-ma-pa, ma-pa-dha, pa-dha-ni, dha-ni-sa.

The varna named Kokila is like the lion's backward glance:
sa-ri-ga, sa-ri-ga-ma — such is its manner.*
notes: "The lion's backward glance" (siṃhāvalokana) is a turn in which the melody, having moved forward, returns to its beginning, like a lion looking back over the way it has come.

verses_en.text:
In the Parijata:
Sa-ri-ga and sa-ri-ga-ma — from these Kokila arises.
Example: sa-ri-ga sa-ri-ga-ma, ri-ga-ma ri-ga-ma-pa, ga-ma-pa ga-ma-pa-dha, ma-pa-dha ma-pa-dha-ni, pa-dha-ni pa-dha-ni-sa.

All these varna-alankaras on the svaras are sweet;
[He] utters them so that sorrow goes far away.

From the lovely moon-like face of Sri Krishnachandra
nectar seems to flow in the form of varna-alankaras.

Sri Radhika, together with the sakhis headed by Lalita,
sings the varna-alankaras with supremely wondrous delight.

The pride of the gandharvas and the others was shattered;
there is no comparison in the world — so sweet [it is].

Praising everyone, Krishna with a joyful heart
gazes with unblinking eyes at Rai's face.

Graha-svara, amsha-svara and nyasa-svara — these three —
Krishna, the abode of rasa, playfully reveals.

Now [it is told] of the graha-svara:
The svara among the seven that is placed at the beginning of a song and the like —
that the sages Bharata and others call the graha-svara.

Thus [it is said]:
That is called the graha-svara which is placed at the beginning of a song and the like.

And in the Sangita-parijata:
That which is set at the beginning of a song and the like is called the graha-svara.

Now [it is told] of the amsha-svara:
The amsha-svara reveals anuraga in song;
Bharata and others thus describe its great power.

Thus [it is said]:
That which in song reveals charm, which all [the others] follow,
which itself becomes graha in the use of nyasa and the rest,
which abounds everywhere — that amsha, the vadi, is like a king.*
notes: The vadi ("the sounding one") is the chief tone of a raga; here it is identified with the amsha-svara.

verses_en.text: "The vadi is that which determines the raga and the rest," [says] the author of the Gita-prakasha. By the words "which itself becomes graha" it is meant that the amsha-svara is the cause of the graha-svara.*
notes: Not in the 1960 edition. The Gita-prakasha is a treatise on music.

verses_en.text:
And further:
Those that are called the life of the ragas the wise call amsha-svaras.

In the Sangita-parijata:
That which abounds in use is called the amsha-svara.*
notes: So in the 1912/13 edition. In the 1960 edition the attributions are transposed: verse 2705 is assigned to the Sangita-parijata, and 2706 is introduced with "And further."

verses_en.text:
Now [it is told] of the nyasa-svara:
The nyasa-svara brings a song and the like to completion;
he who knows this attains bliss.

Thus [it is said]:
The nyasa-svara is declared to be that which completes a song and the like.

Likewise in the Sangita-parijata:
The nyasa-svara should be known as that which concludes a song.

O Srinivasa! Krishna, absorbed in the rapture of rasa,
reveals the arrangement of the graha-, amsha- and nyasa-svaras.

So that Shiva, Brahma and others are astonished,
He spreads forth the svaras, the jatis and the rest.

Now [it is told] of jati:
That from which a raga is born is called jati;
it is the mother of the raga; further, the kinds of jati are three.

That called shuddha, that called vikrita, and from the union of these two
that called sankirna — these three the wise speak of.*
notes: Shuddha means "pure," vikrita "modified," sankirna "mixed."

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said]:
That from which the raga is born is here jati; she is also the mother of the raga.
[She is] threefold: called shuddha, vikrita, and from the union of the two, sankirnaka.

The seven shuddha jatis are named after the svaras, shadja and the rest;
those born of the shuddha are vikrita, say the learned.

Those called vikrita are eleven, the shastras determine;
the remaining, called sankirna, are born of the vikrita.

Shuddha and vikrita — these are eighteen kinds;
these two [kinds] the acharyas accepted.

The shuddha jatis bear the names Shadji, Arshabhi and so on;
the vikrita bear the names Shadja-kaishiki and so on.

Shadja-kaishiki is born from the union of Shadji and Gandhari;
so [arise] those called vikrita — [this] is known everywhere.

Thus [it is said]:
The shuddha jatis are seven; they are named after the svaras, shadja and the rest.
They themselves [become] vikrita; the remaining are born of the mixture of the vikrita.

Others [say]: "Thus [the jatis] are twofold." This was stated by Harinayaka:
"Taken together, the shuddha and the vikrita jatis are declared to be eighteen;
they are the mothers of the ragas."
This very view seems to be the principal one, since it was accepted by the ancient acharyas.*
notes: The words "Others [say]: 'Thus [the jatis] are twofold'" are not in the 1960 edition. Harinayaka is the author of a treatise on music. The eighteen are the seven shuddha and the eleven vikrita (2722–2725).

verses_en.text:
This is stated in another treatise:
Shadji, Arshabhi, Gandhari, Madhyami and likewise Panchami,
Dhaivati and then Naishadi — these seven are the shuddha jatis.

There are Shadja-kaishiki, and after it Shadja-madhyama,
Gandhara-panchami, Andhri, and likewise Shadjodichyavati,*
notes: A (by the scan: «গান্ধারী পঞ্চমান্ধ্রীচ ষড়্জাপি চবতী তথা») and B read ṣaḍjāpi cavatī, the 1960 edition ṣaḍjāpi dhaivatī ("and also Shadja and Dhaivati"); the reading is corrupt. Translated as ṣaḍjodīcyavatī: Dhaivati has already been named among the shuddha (2722), and in the treatises Shadjodichyavati is among the eleven vikrita.

verses_en.text:
Karmavari, Nandayanti, and also Gandharodichchara,
Madhyamodichchara, Rakta-gandhari and also Kaishiki.*
notes: So in all copies (kārmāvarī, gāndhārodīccarā, madhyamodīccarā); the treatises usually have Karmaravi, Gandharodichyava, Madhyamodichyava.

verses_en.text:
Thus eleven vikrita are declared by Bharata and others.
Now we shall state the causes [of the origin] of the vikrita formed from the shuddha.*
notes: The 1960 edition's paraphrase takes śuddhā-siddhā-vikṛtānām as "the shuddha, siddha and vikrita"; cf. 2726, where the vikrita are derived from the union of shuddha.

verses_en.text:
From the union of Shadji and Gandhari is born Shadja-kaishiki;
from Shadji and Madhyami is born Shadja-madhyama;
from Gandhari and Panchami is born Gandhara-panchami — and so on.

The kinds of connection of these eighteen with the gramas
Bharata and other authors of books have described in detail.

From shruti at the beginning to jati at the end — [all] I have told briefly;
know that all this is in part made manifest on the vina.

Thus [it is said]:
Whatever I have set forth, beginning with shruti and ending with jati,
all that the wise may know in part only on the vinas, and not otherwise.

The jatis, mothers of the ragas, took embodied form in the rasa dance;
they deem [this] their own good fortune — there is no end to telling.

O Srinivasa! The rasa pastime is above all;
who knows how to tell what the sweetness of [that] song is like?

The sound of the voices of Rai and Kanu, surpassing the sound of the vina,
reveals the jatis, at which the sakhis rejoice.

When [They] reveal the ragas, each one separately,
what delight increases — who can describe it?

Now [it is told] of raga:
Bharata and others give this definition of raga:
the ragas tinge [with delight] the hearts of [beings] in the three worlds.

Sixteen thousand ragas the shastras determine;
all of them shine on the four sides of Meru.*
notes: So in the 1960 edition (sahasra, cf. the verse 2738); the 1888 and 1912/13 editions have sahaja ("natural"), probably a misprint. Meru is the world mountain at the centre of the universe.

verses_en.text:
Among all these ragas thirty-six ragas
are renowned in the world — so say all the knowers.

Thus [it is said]:
Those by which the hearts of those dwelling in the three worlds are tinged [with delight]
are called ragas — [so say] the sages Bharata and others.

In the Narada-panchama-sara-samhita:*
Krishna began sangita, enchanting [all] with the sound of the flute;
in Krishna's presence the gopis began to sing, each one [her own song];
from that sixteen thousand ragas were born.
notes: The Narada-panchama-sara-samhita is a treatise on music ascribed to Narada; the 1960 edition has Narada-panchama-samhita.

verses_en.text:
And further:
Of these ragas, thirty-six ragas are renowned in the world;
and all of them, too, abide on the four sides of Meru, [say] some.

Of the thirty-six: six ragas and thirty raginis;
each raga has five wives — this too is well accepted.*
notes: Raginis are female ragas, the "consorts" of the male ragas.

verses_en.text:
The six ragas are Bhairava and the rest; in order, for these six,
the raginis are Bhairavi and the rest, known in the shastras.

Thus [it is said] in the Sangita-damodara:
Bhairava, then Vasanta, the raga Malava-kaishika,
the raga Shri, the raga Megha and likewise Nata-narayana.*
notes: In the 1888 edition this verse is preceded by a further half-verse: "Only six ragas are named, and thirty raginis."

verses_en.text:
These are the six male ragas; in order I shall name their raginis:
Bhairavi, Kaishiki, and also Bhasha, Velavali*
notes: So in the 1912/13 edition (bhāṣā); the 1960 edition has Vibhasha.

verses_en.text:
and Vangali — these raginis are here the beloveds of Bhairava.
Andolita, Deshakhya, Lola, Prathama-manjari
and Mallari — these raginis always follow Vasanta.

Gauri, Gunakiri, and also Varadi and Kshamavati
and Karnati — these raginis are dear to Malava-kaishika.

Gandhari, Deva-gandhari, Malavashri, Savari
and also Ramakiri — these raginis are dear to the raga Shri.

Lalita, Malasi, Gauri, Nati and likewise Devakiri —
these raginis are the raga Megha's own beloveds.

Taramani, Svadhabhiri, Kamodi and likewise Gurjari
and Kakubha — these raginis are dear to Nata-narayana.

Some say: six ragas and thirty-six raginis,
each raga has six wives — and this too is quite consistent [with the shastras].

Thus [it is said] in the Narada-panchama-sara-samhita:
The ragas are six, and the raginis thirty-six, of lovely form.
The raga consists of Shiva and Shakti; [it is] an ocean of the rasa of supreme prema:
by merely hearing it Vishnu melted.

Among them, the ragas:
Malava, Mallara, the raga Shri and Vasantaka,
then Hindola and Karnata — [thus] the six male ragas are celebrated.*
notes: The names in 2751–2757 follow the 1912/13 edition (checked against the scan of A); the 1960 edition has Sindhuda (2752), Purabi, Kanada, Koda (2753), Veloyari, Vairagi (2754), Pahida (2756).

verses_en.text:
Dhanasi, Malasi, Ramakeri and likewise Sindhura,
Ashavari and Bhairavi — these are dear to Malava.

Velavali, Pravara, Kanadi and likewise Madhavi,
Kodi and Kedarika — these are dear to Mallara.

Velapari, Gauri, Gandhari and likewise Subhaga,
Kaumari and Vairati — these are dear to the raga Shri.

Todi, Panchami, Lalita, Patha-manjari,
Gurjari and Vibhasha — these are dear to Vasanta.

Mayuri, Dipika, Deshakari and Pahada,
Varadi and Marahatta — these are the wives of Hindola.

Natika, then Bhupali, Ramakeri and likewise Gada,
Kamodi, then Kalyani — these are dear to Karnata.

Thus the learned speak in various ways;
this is reconciled by the fact that different kalpas are meant.

In different lands the ragas bear different names;
no one can give an [exact] determination of the ragas.

Thus [it is said]:
The truth of the ragas, which bear different names in different lands,
no one can determine — neither with the vina, nor I.*
notes: The 1960 edition's paraphrase takes vīṇayā as "she who holds the vina," that is, Sarasvati.

verses_en.text:
The knowers of music determine three kinds of ragas:
sampurna, shadava and audava — these three.*
notes: Sampurna ("full") is a raga of seven svaras, shadava one of six, audava one of five.

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said]:
Among them, sampurna, shadava and audava — thus those ragas are threefold.

Among them, the sampurna:
The ragas that are sung with seven svaras
the knowers of song call sampurna.

Thus [it is said]:
Among them, the sampurna are those that are born from seven svaras.

Those with seven svaras are "sampurna": these ragas are called full;
there are many — the raga Shri, Nata, Karnata and others.

Thus [it is said]:
These — the raga Shri, Nata, Karnata, Gupta-vasantaka,
Shuddha-bhairava, Vangala, the raga Soma, Amra-panchama,

Kamoda, the raga Megha and likewise Dravida-gaudaka,
Varati, Gurjari, Todi, Malavashri and Saindhavi

(Malavashri means Malasi, Saindhavi means Sindhuda),
Devakri, Ramakri and likewise Prathama-manjari,
Nata, Velavali, Gauri and others are held to be sampurna.
(By the words "and others" other [ragas] too, Nata and the rest, are included.)

This is stated in the Sangita-sara:
Nata, Ghantarava, Natta-narayanaka and Bhupati,
and also Shankarabharana — these are held to be full ragas.*
notes: So in the 1888 and 1912/13 editions (nāṭa-ghaṇṭāravo); the 1960 edition has "Nata, Ghanta-raga." Bhūpatī is the reading of G and C; B has bhūpakṣī.

verses_en.text:
The fruit of singing these sampurna ragas is immense;
this is known everywhere; [so] the knowers of music determine.

Thus [it is said] in the Kohaliya:*
Long life, dharma, fame, renown, intelligence, happiness and wealth,
increase of the kingdom, offspring — arise from the full ragas.
notes: The Kohaliya is a treatise ascribed to Kohala (see 2493).

verses_en.text:
The forms of the ragas sampurna and the rest, the kinds of rasa and the rest —
what can be said? All this is [set forth] at length in the shastras.

Among the sampurna and the rest, certain ragas some sing
the other way round; by the difference of kalpas that too is true.

Now [it is told] of the shadava:
All the ragas that arise from six svaras
the knowers of music call shadava.

Thus [it is said]:
The ragas that arise from six svaras are called shadava.

Gauda, Karnata-gauda and other ragas are among the shadava;
the knowers of sangita say that in singing them there is much fruit.

Thus [it is said]:
Gauda, Karnata-gauda, Deshi, and likewise Dhannasika,
Kolahala, Ballali, Desha, Ashavari, and likewise*
notes: Here and below are names of ragas. Dhannasika is the raga Dhanashri. Deśākhyāśāvarī is taken, as in the 1960 edition's paraphrase, as two ragas: Desha (deśākhyā, "called Desha") and Ashavari.

verses_en.text:
Khambavati, Harshapuri, Mallari, then Hunchika —
these and others are declared shadava, in the opinion of Harinayaka.*
notes: Harinayaka is a medieval theorist of music (cf. 2789, 2827, 2842).

verses_en.text:
By the words "and others," others too are included — Shrikantha and the rest. As it is said in the Sangita-sara:
Shrikantha, and also Bhauli, Tara, Shalaga, Gaudaka,
Shuddha-abhiri, Madhukari, Chhaya and Nilotpala —
so in the enumeration of the shadava.*
notes: Tārā-ṣālaga-gauḍakaḥ: so in A (by the scan: «শ্রীকণ্ঠশ্চৈব ভৌলীচ তারাষালগগৌড়কঃ») and the 1960 edition; taken as three ragas: Tara, Shalaga, Gaudaka.

verses_en.text:
Kohala tells the fruit:
Valour in battle, beauty, loveliness, the praise of one's virtues
[come from] singing the shadava ragas — so the ancient sages have declared.

Now the audava.
The ragas that arise from five svaras are audava;
the wise name many ragas among the audava.*
notes: Audava is a raga of five svaras, as shadava is a raga of six (2774–2780).

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said]:
Those which are born of five svaras are known as audava.

Madhyamadi, Mallara and other ragas are among the audava;
much fruit is gained in this audava singing.

Thus [it is said]:
Madhyamadi, Mallara, Deshapala, Malava,
Hindola, Bhairava, Nagadhvani, and likewise Gondakriti,

then Lalita, Chhaya, Todi, and likewise Velavali;
Saindhavi with "Pratapa" before it is named, and likewise the second;
these and others are declared audava — ragas that captivate people's hearts.*
notes: That is, the raga Pratapa-saindhavi (the 1960 edition's paraphrase has "Pratapasindhu"); "the second" is apparently a second variety of Saindhavi.

verses_en.text:
By the words "and others," Turushka, Gauda and the rest are also included. As it is said in the Sangita-sara in the enumeration of the audava:
Turushka, Gauda, Gandhara, Pulinda, Megharanjaka — so.*
notes: The copies read turaska (G), turakṣa (A, B, C); the usual form is turuṣka, Turushka.

verses_en.text:
Kohala tells the fruit:
To destroy disease, to destroy enemies, to dispel fear and grief,
and in rites for pacifying the planets, the audava should be sung.

Now the sankirna.
The ragas that have been described, through mutual mixing,
the wise call sankirna; in them is beauty for the ear.*
notes: Sankirna ("mixed") ragas are those arising from the union of two or more ragas (2790).

verses_en.text:
On this Harinayaka [says]:
From the mutual mixing of these ragas [arise] a great many names;
some of them, beautiful to the ear, are called sankirna.

Pauravi, Kalyani and others are called sankirna;
the meaning of "sankirna" is: made of the union of two, three or more ragas.

Here, Pauravi.
From parts of Deshi and Mallari [comes the raga] that bears the name Pauravi;
thus the wise reveal these easily grasped ragas.

Thus [it is said]:
From parts of [the raga] called Desha and of Mallarika
arises this Pauravi — so it is taught.

Kalyani:
From [the ragas] called Varati, Nata and Karnataka
arose this charming [raga] called Kalyanika.

Saranga:
Saranga arises from Todi and Dhannasika.

Gauri:
From the raga Shri and the raga Gauda arises Gauri.

Nata-mallarika:
Born of parts of Nata and Mallaraka
is Nata-mallarika.

Vallavi:
From the union of Desha and Ashavari, it is declared, [arises] Vallavi.

Karnatika:
From parts of Karnata and Bhairava
[arises the raga] called Karnatika, [sung] with a quiver of the voice.

Mukhavari:
From the union of Saindhavi and Todika arose Mukhavari.*
notes: So in A (by the scan: «সমুৎপন্না মুখাবরী»), B, C (mukhāvarī); the 1960 edition has Sukhavari (sukhāvarī).

verses_en.text:
Ashavari:
From the union of Mallara, Saindhavi and Todi arises Ashavari.

Ramakeli:
From the union of Gurjari and Deshika was born Ramakeli.

There are many other ragas too with the marks of sankirna;
as each is heard in [a given] land, so the wise should know it.

The times at which each of these ragas is fit to be sung —
all those times are stated in the shastras of sangita.

Singing out of [its] time is a fault in the singer;
singing the raga Gurjari and the like destroys that fault.

Thus [it is said]:
Transgressing the [proper] time in singing surely brings ruin to all;
[but] in group singing, at the king's command and on the stage it brings no fault.*
notes: So in G (raṅga-bhūmau, "on the stage"); the 1912/13 edition (by the scan of A: «বঙ্গভূমৌ») has vaṅga-bhūmau ("in the land of Banga"), apparently a misprint.

verses_en.text:
And those who, out of greed and delusion, or in separation, sing [out of time] —
their fault, it is said, the sweet Gurjari destroys.

Vasanta, Ramakeli, Gurjari — these three:
singing [them] at any time gives rise to no fault.

Thus [it is said] in the Ratna-mala:
Vasanta, Ramakeli, and also the sweet Gurjari —
[when] they are sung at any time, no fault whatever arises.

Narada, however, states a particular rule:
At night, after ten dandas have passed, the singing of all [ragas] is enjoined.*
notes: A danda is a measure of time of 24 minutes; ten dandas are four hours.

verses_en.text:
All these ragas, taking on form, attentively
consider themselves blessed in the rasa-mandala.

What shall I say, O Srinivasa! In the Sri rasa-mandala,
from the singing of various ragas an ocean of joy surges up.

This singing has no equal in all the world;
supreme, wondrous nectar [they] shower upon one another.

Krishna, gazing at the lotus face of Rai,
reveals in song so much wondrous skill!

The characteristics of song were partly stated before;
now learn how the kinds of song were revealed.

Song is of two kinds — anibaddha and nibaddha;
anibaddha, as it is defined, has the form of the alapa of a raga.*
notes: Anibaddha ("unbound") is free singing not held together by bandha (construction from parts, metre and words); nibaddha ("bound") is song built from dhatus and angas (2838). Alapa is the unhurried unfolding of a raga without tala.

verses_en.text:
Song devoid of bandha is anibaddha;
the alapa of a raga is said to be the manifesting of the raga.

Thus [it is said]:
Song, it is declared, is twofold: anibaddha and nibaddha;
alapti is without bandha; it has the form of the alapa of a raga.

On this it is said:
Because alapti is devoid of bandha, it is called anibaddha.
"The alapa of a raga" means its manifesting.

Varnalankara in alapa is of two kinds:
one is "a-ta-na-ri," the other "sa-ri-ga-ma" and the rest.*
notes: Varnalankara is ornamentation with syllables: meaningless syllables ("a-ta-na-ri" and the like) or the names of the svaras (sa, ri, ga, ma, pa, dha, ni); see 2824, 2828.

verses_en.text:
These four [syllables] "a-ta-na-ri" are merely hunkara;
in order they denote Hari, Gauri, Hara and Brahma.*
notes: Hunkara is the sound "hum," an inarticulate utterance of the voice. Hara is Shiva; Gauri is his consort.

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said] in the Narada-samhita and other [books]:
As from hunkara the Veda is born — in the form of "Om,"
[so here]: by the word "ta" Gauri is meant, by the word "na" Hara is meant;
the sounds "ta-na" rise gradually from the hunkara.

And there too:
By the sound "a" Hari is designated, by the sound "ri" the Grandsire;
in the word "a-ta-na-ri" is the manifestation of them all.

Sa, ri, ga, ma, pa, dha, ni — the seven varnalankaras;
the svaras beginning with shadja — this is varnalapa; so it is known.

In alapa the places of the gamakas are exceedingly varied;
in it are many charming nuances — this is well known.*
notes: A gamaka is a melodic ornament (oscillation, sliding of the tone).

verses_en.text:
All that [is sung] without tala enters into alapa;
the knowers of song name countless kinds of alapa.

Harinayaka, however, [says]:
Joined with varnalankaras, adorned with the places of the gamakas,
charming with many nuances — [such] is called alapti by the knowers.

By this [it is meant] that all that [is sung] without tala enters into alapa. Varnalankara, moreover, is meaningless sounds such as hunkara, and the varnalankara "sa-ri-ga-ma" and so on, named in [the teaching of] sangita.
The kinds of alapti are many; for fear of prolixity they are not stated.

O Srinivasa! In the midst of the Sri rasa-mandali
all perform alapa in countless ways.

Whom would that alapa not astonish?
What is the paltry kokila before the sound of those voices!

At the time of alapa there is wondrous play:
each displays their own skill.

Krishna, the crest-jewel of rasikas, performs alapa on the flute;
He intoxicates the world — what can it be compared to?

On the vina the Queen of Vrindavana performs alapa;
who can describe the sweetness of Her alapa?*
notes: The Queen of Vrindavana (Vrindavaneshvari) is Radha.

verses_en.text:
Lalita and the other sakhis perform alapa on various instruments;
what to speak of others — hearing it, stone melts.

Who could tell of the alapa with one mouth?
It surges up like the waves of an ocean of nectar.

Immersed in anibaddha singing, they with one another
perform nibaddha song in various ways.

Now nibaddha is described.
When [song] is bound by dhatus and angas, it is called nibaddha;
nibaddha is these three: shuddha, chhayalaga, kshudra.*
notes: Angas are the component parts of a song. Shuddha ("pure"), chhayalaga ("bearing the shadow [of another]") and kshudra ("small") are the three kinds of nibaddha. So in G (chāyālaga); A (by the scan: «শুদ্ধা, ছায়া নগ ক্ষুদ্র», «ছায়া নগং»), B, C have "ছায়া নগ" (chāyā naga), apparently a misprint of the old editions.

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said]:
That which is bound by dhatus and angas is called nibaddha;
and it is held to be threefold: shuddha, chhayalaga, kshudra.

Here shuddha is described.
That which is joined with alapa, dhatus and angas is shuddha;
alapa here is defined as meaningful words.

Thus [it is said]:
That which is joined with alapas, dhatus and angas is called shuddha.
The knowers of the tradition [say] that by "alapas" here meaningful words alone [are meant].
Harinayaka, however, says that alapa is the alapti of gamakas devoid of syllables.

The three kinds of nibaddha song have been defined;
some name [them] thus: shuddha, salaga, sankirna.*
notes: Salaga (in the treatises usually sālaga) is the same as chhayalaga; sankirna here is kshudra (2844).

verses_en.text:
In the Sangita-sara:
By the distinction of shuddha, salaga and sankirna, song is held to be threefold.
Here by the word "sankirna" kshudra alone is meant.
For it is said by the same [author]: "And it is threefold: shuddhaka, chhayalaga, kshudraka."

Some say: nibaddha song has three names —
prabandha, vastu, rupaka; this is well known.

If in it there are four dhatus and six angas,
then [this] excellent construction is called prabandha.*
notes: A play on words: prabandha — prakṛṣṭa bandha, "excellent construction."

verses_en.text:
The wise call shuddha song prabandha;
now learn the characteristics of vastu and rupaka.

With three dhatus and the rest and with five angas, vastu is defined;
with two dhatus and two angas, it is called rupaka.*
notes: Prabandha, vastu and rupaka are three names for a song composition (nibaddha): prabandha has four dhatus and six angas, vastu three dhatus and five angas, rupaka two dhatus and two angas (see 2850–2852). The angas are the constituent elements of a song (see 2872–2884).

verses_en.text:
[The words] of Harinayaka:*
Nibaddha has three names: prabandha, vastu, rupaka.
notes: Harinayaka is the author of a Sanskrit treatise on music, to whom Narahari refers many times. Nibaddha ("bound") is a song bound by a fixed text, metre and tala. In 2851 there is a play on the word "prabandha": prakṛṣṭa bandha, "an excellent binding."

verses_en.text:
That composition which is bound with four dhatus, formed with six angas
and excellent is called prabandha.

(Thereby it is said that prabandha is shuddha song itself.)
With three and more dhatus and with five angas it is called vastu;
with two dhatus and likewise with two angas it is celebrated as rupaka.

Now on dhatu:
The component part (avayava) of a prabandha is defined as dhatu;
know that a particular part is called avayava.*
notes: Here dhatu is a section (part) of a composition, not the melodic side of a song as in 2530–2535.

verses_en.text:
Some say: the dhatus are four — udgrahaka, and
melapaka, dhruva, abhoga — in this order it is established.

Udgraha is first, melapaka comes after it,
after that dhruva, at the end abhoga — these are the four.*
notes: Udgraha ("taking up") is the opening section of a song, melapaka ("the joining one") the transition, dhruva ("the constant one") the recurring refrain, abhoga ("completion") the concluding section; antara ("the intermediate one," 2861–2862) is the section between dhruva and abhoga.

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said]:
The component part of a prabandha is dhatu; it is declared to be fourfold:
udgrahaka, melapaka, dhruva and abhoga — in order.

Udgraha is the first part; then, it is taught, melapaka;
after [it] dhruva, [so called] because of its constancy; and abhoga is held to be the last.

In defining prabandha some assert thus:
udgraha, dhruva, abhoga — these three are the dhatus.

The first line of a song is called udgraha;
dhruva is in the middle, and at the end abhoga is defined.

Thus [it is said] in the [Sangita-]shiromani:
Udgraha is the first line, as the ancient teachers have said;
dhruva, [so called] because of its constancy, is in the middle, and abhoga, it is taught, is the last.
"Because of its constancy" means because of its fixedness, [since it] is taken up again and again.*
notes: This explanatory line is in the 1912/13 edition (B); it is absent from the 1960 edition.

verses_en.text:
The line that is between dhruva and abhoga
the knowers call the dhatu named antara.

Thus it is said by Harinayaka:
Arising between dhruva and abhoga is another dhatu, called antara.

In the abhoga come the names of the poet and the hero;
for this reason the knowers of song give [it] the name "abhoga."

Thus [it is said]:
In the abhoga is the name of the poet, and likewise the name of the hero.

Such as the dhatus in a prabandha are, such is their definition;
the knowers of song display [them] in various songs.

An example in a song — [the raga] Patamanjari:*
The full moon has risen in the night,
its rays drive the darkness far away.
The expanse of the bank of the Daughter of the Sun
shines with abundant whiteness. (Udgraha.)
notes: The song 2866–2871 (in Brajabuli) illustrates the dhatus of a prabandha; the names of the sections are given in the text itself. All copies read পঠমঞ্জরী (paṭhamañjarī); the usual name of the raga is Patamanjari (paṭamañjarī).

verses_en.text:
Gently, gently blows the fragrant,
cool breeze from Malaya.
Swarms of bees hum densely; how many
cuckoos and parrots call! (Melapaka.)

The Youth of Vraja sports:
seeing the sweet charm of the Vrinda forest,
[He] is utterly enraptured. (Dhruva.)

Today in the beautiful rasa-mandala, unattainable [even] for the gods, there is great merriment.
Taking the flute in [His] hand, [He] touches [it] to [His] lips; joy fills [His] heart.

Excellent songs of many kinds, full of Radhika's qualities and deeds, [He] composes;
absorbed in singing, [He shows] an incomparable manner that steals all the pride of the Lord of Rati. (Antara.)

In the graceful play of [His] lotus eyes [He] pours forth rasa like a cloud [pouring rain].
What shall Ghanashyama tell? Incomparable love has become manifest in the world. (Abhoga.)*
notes: Ghanashyama is the author's second name, Narahari's; according to 2863–2864, the poet's name is given in the abhoga.

verses_en.text:
Now on the angas:
The dhatus of a prabandha are five — so the shastras determine.
Prabandha song with six angas is current everywhere.*
notes: The five dhatus are udgraha, melapaka, dhruva, antara and abhoga.

verses_en.text:
Svara, biruda, pada, tenaka, patha, tala —
with these six angas a song is supremely sweet.*
notes: Svara is the notes (sa, ri, ga…); biruda is laudatory epithets naming qualities; pada is meaningful words; tenaka (tena) is the auspicious syllables "tena"; patha is syllables imitating the sound of instruments (drums); tala is the rhythmic cycle.

verses_en.text:
Svara is defined as sa, ri, ga, ma, pa, dha and the rest;
[words] joined with the names of qualities are, in [this] teaching, called biruda.

Pada is words that express [meaning]; of this there are many kinds.
Words such as "tena," "tena" are for the sake of auspiciousness.

Patha is the syllables born of instruments: "dha," "dha," "dhilanga" and the like;
tala is chachchatputa, yati and the rest, according to the rules.*
notes: Chachchatputa, yati and adi (2881) are names of talas.

verses_en.text:
These six angas the ancient acharyas define;
some name four: words, svara, tala and tena.

Thus [it is said]:
The six angas of a prabandha are svara, biruda, pada,
tenaka, patha and tala. The svaras are sa, ri, ga, ma and the rest.

That which [serves] to mention qualities is declared to be biruda;
and that which expresses something else is called pada.

The word "tena" is tena; it is determined as having the sense of auspiciousness.
"Dham dham," "dhuga-dhuga" and the like are the pathas, the multitudes of instrumental syllables.
Adi, yati and the rest are the talas; and tala will be described [later].

In the Sangita-parijata:
Pada, tala, svara, patha, tena and [what] is called biruda —
these are the six angas of song, named by the wise.

Padas are words that express [meaning]; the talas are chachchatputa and the rest;
the svaras are shadja and the rest; patha is a syllable born of an instrument;
tena is an auspicious word; biruda is [a word] joined with the names of qualities.

The jatis of prabandha are five: medini, nandini,
dipani, pavani, taravali — so says the muni.*
notes: Here jati is a class of prabandha by the number of its angas (compare the other sense of the word in 2541–2543). The muni, according to the 1960 edition, is Bharata.

verses_en.text:
[A prabandha] with six angas is named medini, with five angas nandini,
with four angas dipani, and this one, with three angas, pavani.

With two angas it is taravali, say the knowers of song.
Hence know: a prabandha with one anga is not accepted.

Thus [it is said]:
The jatis of prabandhas are five, approved by the sages:
medini, nandini, dipani, and also pavani

and taravali. Now their characteristics are set forth:
medini is said to have six angas, nandini five,

dipani has four angas, pavani is held to have three,
taravali, as the ancient knowers of song have said, has two.
(By this it is established that there is no prabandha with one anga.)

In the Sangita-parijata:
The jatis of prabandhas are five, and they [follow] in order:
with six angas there is medini, with five nandini;

with four it is called dipani, with three angas pavani;
with two angas the jati taravali arises.

The varieties of shuddha prabandha have no end;
the knowers of sangita define [them] in various ways.

Thus [it is said]:
Because of the endlessness of shuddha prabandhas, their variety is indeed only one.

Even so:
with one tala, with two instruments, with three or with many,
a good poet may certainly compose prabandhas as he wishes.*
notes: All copies (A by the scan: «তালেনৈকেন বাদ্যাভ্যাং ত্রিভির্বা») read vādyābhyām ("with two instruments"); from the sense (compare "prabandhas with many talas" in 2896) dvābhyām ("with two [talas]") is possible.

verses_en.text:
Moreover:
prabandhas with many talas are to be composed with many ragas
or with one raga — according to the rules for patha and the rest.
Their varieties are very many; who will tell of them completely?

Therefore it is said:
Neither to ragas, nor to talas, nor, especially, to instruments,
nor even to prabandha songs is there an end in the world.

O Srinivasa! Krishna with His beloveds in the rasa dance
reveals shuddha prabandha, unattainable for Brahma and the others.

Seeing the beauty of Rai and Kanu, absorbed in song,
Vrinda-devi in her bliss cannot restrain her heart.

[She] bids the shukas, sharis and cuckoos
to describe the glory of the qualities of Sri Krishna and Radhika.*
notes: The shuka is a parrot, the shari his mate (a female parrot or myna), and the cuckoo (pika) the Indian koel. The birds sing songs of the medini (2903–2907, 2908–2911) and nandini (2912–2914) types, which contain the angas: words, biruda epithets, svaras ("sa ri ga"), tena ("tenna"), patha ("dha dha"); syllables without meaning are rendered by their sound.

verses_en.text:
At Vrinda's bidding the delighted shukas, sharis and cuckoos
describe the qualities of Sri Krishna and Radhika.

The shuka says — an example of a medini song with six angas:
Glory, glory! Delighter of the people, lotus-eyed,
the young nagara like dense collyrium, e e!
Taker of family fidelity from the noble [wives] of Gokula,
moon-faced, ocean of virtues, e e!

Son of Nanda, ornament of Vraja, full of rasa,
with charming arms, increaser of joy, e e!
Treasure of the heart of the daughter of Sri Vrishabhanu,
crusher of the pride of myriads of Madanas, e e!

Skilled in song, delighting in the ways of Nidhuvana,
incomparable master of the tandava dance, e e!
In the expanse of the courtyard — the bank of the Daughter of the Sun —
adorned with jewels, the hosts of lovely women, e e!

Holder of the flute, holder of the mountain, with graceful
red lips, beautiful, e e!
With teeth [like] kunda jasmine, charming, slender-waisted,
the Purandara of the Vrinda forest, e e!

Krishna, the foremost champion of love-quarrels,
dha dha dhi dhi ta ga dhenna e e!
Sa sa ri ga ri — the Lord of Narahari,
e i a iti ai ai atenna e e!

The shari says — an example of a medini song:
Glory! Worshipped by the world, the renowned princess,
Radhika, moon-faced, dispeller of sorrow!
Delighter of Shyama's heart, breaker of [His] firm composure,
with doe's eyes that put to shame the lotus, the khanjana and the fish!

Whose luster has conquered the lightning, supremely charming, the beautiful lady,
crusher of the pride of the Daughter of the Ocean and others,
with a lovely gentle smile, with graceful sweet speech, enchantress of the world,
increaser of the joy of Lalita and the others!*
notes: The Daughter of the Ocean is Lakshmi.

verses_en.text:
Lovely in the adornment of love, [in] pastimes ever new and new,
the delight of the Vrinda forest, with an elephant's gait,
rapt in the rasa of the rasa dance, a river of sweetness,
the jewel of all women, the mistress of Narahari!

Jhanta jham jhanta takha vitakato thunna drimiki
trigao takata ta thaiya.
Sari rigama pamaga manma gari sas sati ai
tenna tenna tenam ti ai e a.*
notes: The syllables are given after G and B, checked against the scan of A («ঝান্তা ঝাং ঝান্তা তাথা বিত কতো থুন্না দৃমিকি ত্রিগও তকতা তা থৈয়া»); G "বান্তা বাং ঝান্তা তাখা বিতকতো থুন্না দৃমকি ত্রিগও তকতা তা থৈয়া," B "ঝাসন্তা ঝাং ঝান্তা তাখা বিত কতো থুন্না দুমিকি…".

verses_en.text:
The cuckoo says — an example of a nandini song with five angas:
Glory, glory, Krishna, merciful Keshava,
lotus-eyed, delighter of the people, a!
Elephant in the lotus forest of young maidens, charming
khanjana in the cage of the beloved's heart, a!

With a sweet smile on the lovely moon of the face,
breaker of the weight of Radha's composure, a!
Beautiful, best of dancers, son of Nanda,
collyrium for the eyes of ever new young maidens, a!

Sari gama gama pama manmama garisa
tenna tennati ati ai iya.
Ai, increaser of Narahari's joy, e e,
ai ati ai tiya.

O Srinivasa! The birds in various ways
sing the fair fame of Radha and Krishna in shuddha songs.

The varieties of song prabandhas cannot be told;
the shastras define [them] by shakti, varna, particular features and the rest.*
notes: The sense of the word "shakti" (śakti, "power, capacity"; in the 1960 edition শাক্তি) is unclear here; translated literally.

verses_en.text:
Ela and the rest are difficult; among them are twenty-six songs;
what is easy and what is hard in this the shastras have revealed.*
notes: Ela is one of the classical prabandhas (complex song forms); next (2918–2927) twenty-six prabandhas are listed.

verses_en.text:
The first is named Panchataleshvara;
after it come four varieties of Varnasvara:

Varnasvara beginning with svara, Varnasvara beginning with patha,
Varnasvara beginning with pada, Varnasvara beginning with tena.

Next they name the song Svarartha-matrika.
Thus the knowers of song define the twenty-six.

Thus [it is said]:
There are difficult prabandhas — Ela and the rest — spoken of by the sages;
of them twenty-six are named by the learned Harinayaka.

And they are listed in order, by name alone:
Panchataleshvara, Varnasvara and Angacharini,*
notes: The names of the prabandhas are given as in the text; the readings of several are unclear (OCR): স্বরাদ্যকরণং (Svaradya-karana); বর্তন্যথ — B বদ্ধন্যথ, G বত্মস্যিথ, C বর্মন্যথ, understood as vartany atha ("then Vartani"); মাতিলক (possibly Umatilaka); সিংহনীল (possibly Simhalila). Angacharini (aṅga-cāriṇī) may be not a separate name but a qualifier of Varnasvara (compare its four varieties in 2918–2919).

verses_en.text:
and also Svarartha-matrika, Ragakadambaka,
Svaradya-karana, then Vartani, and likewise Talarnava,

Shriranga, Shrivilasa, then Panchabhangi,
Panchanana, Matilaka, and also Simhanila.

Tribhangi, Hamsanila, and also Harivilasaka,
Sudarshana, Svaranga, Shrivardhana, Harshavardhana,

Vira, Shrimangala, and Lahadi is also named;
[the prabandha] called by the name Navaratna is named, and also Sarabhanilaka,*
notes: So in A (by the scan: «লাহড়ী চ প্রকীর্ত্তিতা … তথা সরভনীলকঃ»): "লাহড়ী" (lāhaḍī, Lahadi); "সরভনীলক" (sarabhanīlaka; possibly Sharabhalila — cf. the name of a tala in 2968). Here the list of the twenty-six prabandhas (2921–2927) ends.

verses_en.text:
and the one that is called Kanthabharana: these are held to be the twenty-six.
There are also six others — Chandraprakashaka and the rest.

The characteristics of all these prabandhas are well known;
the poets describe [them] so that all hearts are delighted.

At Vrinda's bidding the bee, with great eagerness,
sings a svarartha prabandha in the guise of humming.

The syllables of the svarartha prabandha are sa, ri, ga, ma and the rest;
in two kinds, shuddha and mishra, [it] expresses [meaning] at will.*
notes: Svarartha ("meaning [from] the svaras") is a prabandha in which the desired meaning is expressed by the syllables of the svaras alone (sa, ri, ga, ma, pa, dha, ni), see 2931; shuddha means "pure," mishra "mixed."

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said]:
Where the desired meaning is expressed by the syllables of the svaras alone,
that [prabandha] is svarartha; it is twofold, by the distinction of shuddha and mishra.
(If by the syllables of the svaras — sa, ri, ga, ma, pa, dha, ni — the desired meaning is expressed at will, then it is svarartha: such is the sense.)

Joyfully the bee reveals the svarartha prabandha;
hearing [it], Sri Lalita and the other sakhis are filled with happiness.

For example — the raga Kedara:*
Glory! Crown of rasikas, Krishna, tender-limbed,
shining like dense collyrium!
With the moon of [Your] face anointed with the nectar of smiles,
making the directions clear with lovely rays!
notes: The indication of the raga ("রাগঃ কেদার") is in B; the 1960 edition does not have it. The song 2933–2936 is an example of the svarartha prabandha sung by the bee (2929–2932).

verses_en.text:
With charming wide eyes that have conquered the lotus,
stealer of the wealth of the young maidens' composure!
Triumphant in Vraja, the young crown prince, the best of dancers,
holder of the flute, with reddish lips!

Crusher of the pride of the Lord of Rati, enjoyer of the sweet rasa dance,
beautiful, incomparable!
Graceful, like a jewel, greedily drawn to the fragrance
of the lotus faces of the jewels among the women of Vraja!*
notes: The second half of the line follows the scan of A: «ব্রজরমণীমণি-মুখপদ্ম পরিমল লুব্ধ বঙ্ক রতন সমা» (lubdha "greedy, enamoured," baṅka "graceful," ratana-samā "like a jewel"; the OCR of copy B has «নিব … সগা»). In the OCR of the 1960 edition this half and the first half of 2936 are lost.

verses_en.text:
King of the new kunjas, subduer of the serpent,
in charming attire of every kind!
Increaser of Ghanashyama's joy — pama gamamma gari
mapa dhani padha nidha!*
notes: Ghanashyama is the author's second name, Narahari. The svara syllables follow the 1960 edition ("পমগমম্মগরি মপধনিপধনিধা"); in B the line is corrupt.

verses_en.text:
Thus Vrinda directs a multitude of birds;
with songs of various prabandhas they all give delight.

O Srinivasa! Krishna with His beloveds in the rasa dance
reveals the highest limit of the prabandhas of shuddha song.

Within shuddha some speak of shuda prabandha;
others reveal shuda within chhayalaga.*
notes: Shuda (in the treatises sūḍa) is a song form woven of many talas (2941–2942).

verses_en.text:
Now, chhayalaga:
Because [it] clings to the shadow of shuddha, it is called "chhayalaga";
in it shuda is composed with talas, instruments and the rest.

The weaving together of many talas — such is the charming shuda;
the term "chhayalaga" has another name, salaga.*
notes: All copies read "সংজ্ঞা রসালগ" (saṃjñā rasālaga); understood as saṃjñār sālaga ("the term… salaga"), cf. 2944. Salaga is the same term as in 2843.

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said]:
That which clings to the shadow of shuddha they know as chhayalaga;
it is charming, composed as shuda with talas, instruments and the rest.
(Shuda is the weaving together of many talas in one: such is the sense. By the words "clings to the shadow" it is said that it arises with some of the characteristics of shuddha: such is the sense.)

It is said of this:
If [in it] there is only a shadow of the features stated [above],
it is to be known as chhayalaga — [so say] the munis Bharata and the others.

(It also has another name, salaga: such is the sense.) Of this Harinayaka has said:
Now, the shuda that [is] chhayalaga is itself salaga.

According to differing views the salaga shudas are many;
and so they define dhruvaka and the rest [as] excellent.

Thus [it is said] in Damodara and in the Panchama-sara-samhita:
Dhruvaka, manthaka, pratimantha, nisharuka,
vasaka, pratitala, and also ekatalika,
yati and jhumari — thus is the salaga shuda named.*
notes: Dhruvaka, manthaka and the rest are kinds of salaga shuda. "বাসক" (vāsaka): so in A (by the scan: «বাসকঃ প্রতিতালশ্চ», «চত্বারো বাসকাঃ»), C and the 1960 edition; possibly the rāsaka of the treatises.

verses_en.text:
[Now] the varieties of dhruvaka and the rest are told:
Dhruvakas are said to be sixteen, manthakas of six kinds,
pratimanthas five, nisharukas are known to be seven;

vasakas are said to be four, pratitalakas four,
ekatali of three kinds, yatis are held to be four;
and jhumari is only one: these are the salagas named.

Some say there are ten other salagas — charcharika and the rest;
thus they, the salagas, come to be nineteen — a multitude.*
notes: The nine kinds (2946) and ten more give nineteen. The 1960 edition reads "ভুবি" ("on earth") instead of "ভুরি" ("a multitude").

verses_en.text:
The characteristics of dhruvaka and the rest are extremely difficult;
shuda in nine talas — it gives joy in every way.

Thus [it is said]:
Adi, yati, nasaru, and also addatala, triputa,
rupaka, jhampaka, mantha, ekatali — so [the talas] are named.*
notes: So in A (by the scan: «আদির্যতির্নসারুশ্চাড্ডতালস্ত্রিপুটস্তথা»): "নসারু" (nasāru; G "ন্সারু"); "চাজ্ঞতাল" is understood as cāḍḍatāla ("and also addatala"); the 1960 edition's translation has "অজ্ঞ" (ajña).

verses_en.text:
That which is composed with these nine talas is called shuda;
such a shuda is charming in singing, in playing instruments and in dance.

The varieties of prabandhas — shuda and the rest — are manifold;
their characteristics, examples and so on are set forth in the shastras.

In song tala is joined; without tala there is no purity —
as it is with a boat without a helmsman.

The derivation of the word "tala" [is explained] in many ways;
the acharyas have made this known.

Thus [it is said]:
Without tala the purity of song does not arise in song and the rest,
as with a boat without a helmsman; therefore we set them forth.*
notes: The 1960 edition reads "গতিশুদ্ধি" ("purity of movement") instead of "গীতশুদ্ধি" ("purity of song").

verses_en.text: Here the acharyas have explained the derivation of the word "tala" in many ways.

Harinayaka [says] of this:
Because by the evenness of time and, moreover, by its charm
it establishes sangita, it is called tala.
("Talayati" — establishes; the root "tal" is in the sense of "establishing.")

But in the Sangita-sara:
"Ta" is Isha, Girija is "la";
hence tala, from the union of Shiva and Shakti.
Or else here "tala" is from the root "tal" with [the suffix] ghañ;
or "tala" is from the union of "ta" and "la."*
notes: Isha ("the Lord") is Shiva; Girija ("Daughter of the Mountain") is Parvati, Shakti. Ghañ is a suffix of Sanskrit grammar.

verses_en.text:
In the Ratna-mala:
"Ta" is Sharajanma, "a" is called Vishnu,
"la" is declared to be Maruta: these gods dwell in the tala.*
notes: Sharajanma ("born in the reeds") is Kartikeya, the son of Shiva; Maruta is the god of the wind. "A" is the long vowel in the word tāla.

verses_en.text:
But Vachaspati [says]:
The action — stretching and bending of the fingers of the hand and the rest —
and the measure of time [set] by it is here called tala.*
notes: Vachaspati is an author whom Narahari cites; his treatise has not been identified.

verses_en.text:
Now [it is told] of the talas:
The talas chachchatputa, chachaputa and the rest are the chief ones;
a hundred and one talas — [this] is accepted everywhere.

Thus [it is said]:
Chachchatputa, chachaputa, and also shatpitaputraka,
sampakveshtaka, udghatta, aditala and darpana,*
notes: The names of the talas follow A/B/C; in the 1960 edition a number of readings differ: "চচ্চৎপুট" (A/C "চঞ্চৎপুট"; the usual chachchatputa is adopted, cf. 2876), "রঙ্গলীল", "হংসলীল", "বর্ণলীল" (A/B/C "-নীল"). Many names are distorted by OCR.

verses_en.text:
charchari, simhanila, kandarpa, simhavikrama,
shriranga, ranganila, rangatala, parikrama,

pratyanga, gajalila, tribhinna, viravikrama,
hamsanila, varnanila, and also rajachudamani,

rangadyota, rajatala, and also simhavikridita,
vanamali, varnatala, mishra, rangapradipaka,

hamsanada, simhanada, the one called mallikamoda,
then sharabhalila and rangabharana,

then turagalila, and after it simhanandana,
jayashri, vijayananda, pratitala, dvitiyaka,

makaranda, kirtitala, vijaya, jayamangala,
rajavidyadhara, mantha, jayatala, sudurbala,*
notes: A (by the scan: «জয়তালঃ সুদুর্ব্বলঃ»), B, C read "সুদুর্বলঃ" (sudurbala); the 1960 edition reads "কুড়ুককঃ" (kuḍukkaka, kudukkaka).

verses_en.text:
then nihsharuka, krida, tribhangi, kokilapriya,
shrikanta, bindumali, samatala and nandana,

udikshana, mallika, dhenkika, varnamanthika,
abhinanda, antarakrida, laghutala and dipaka,

anangatala, vishama, sandikunda and mukundaka,
ekatali, kankala, chatustala and khamkhudi,*
notes: A (by the scan: «সান্দীকুন্দমুকুন্দকৌ»), B and the 1960 edition read "সান্দীকুন্দ" (sāndīkunda), C "নান্দীকুন্দ" (nāndīkunda).

verses_en.text:
abhanga, rajavankara, and also laghushekhara,
and another, pratapashekhara, jagajhampa, chaturmukha,

vankara, pratimantha, and also the tala tritiyaka;
after it, as should be known, vasanta, lalita, shiva,

karashakha, shattala, vardhana, and also vardhaka;
then, as the learned declare, rajanarayana;
madana too should be known, and also parvatilochana.*
notes: Not in the 1960 edition: there the second half of 2975 is "তস্মাদুপরি বিজ্ঞেয়ঃ পার্বতীলোচনস্তথা" (the text between the two occurrences of "বিজ্ঞেয়" is skipped). Text from A (by the scan): «… রাজনারায়ণস্তস্মাদ্বিদ্বদ্ভিঃ পরিকীর্ত্তিতঃ» (vidvadbhiḥ parikīrtitaḥ, "declared by the learned"); «বিদ্বপ্তি» in the OCR of copy B is a distortion, not the name of a tala.

verses_en.text:
Then there is sarangatala, then shrinandivardhana,
and another, lilavilokita, and also lalitapriya,

janaka, lakshmisha, the one called ragavardhana,
and utsava: thus the talas are one more than a hundred.

In Damodara and others some of these are found otherwise;
since the opinions of the rishis are many, what harm is there in variants among them?

The characteristics and examples of all these talas
the knowers of sangita have joyfully made known.

The angas of tala are fivefold, beginning with anudruta, [they] say,
and they define the rules: [how many] matras in laghu and the rest.*
notes: A matra is a unit of time. Anudruta, druta, laghu, guru and pluta are the five angas (measures) of tala: a quarter matra, half a matra, one, two and three matras (2982).

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said]:
Anudruta, druta, laghu, and after it guru
and pluta: thus in order the angas of tala are fivefold.
Apart from anudruta, the names of the others are [from the syllables] da, la, ga, pa.

Laghu is of one matra, guru of two matras,
pluta of three matras, druta of half a matra,
and anudruta of half of druta's matra,
and its name may also be "virama."

Anudruta, druta, laghu, guru, pluta — such are the signs.
(The signs are these: …)*
notes: The signs in A (by the scan): «( আকারো যথা—, ।, ৬, । । ।, )» — apparently some of the signs did not print; the 1960 edition has "লঘু (), গুরু (৬), পুত (0)"; the Bengali translation of the 1960 edition gives laghu "|", guru "৬", pluta "||".

verses_en.text:
[Now] the places of their strokes, with [their] measure, are told:*
Druta is a stroke of the hand [from a height of] four fingers;
la, ga, pa — eight, sixteen, twenty-four.
notes: "সাবধিক" (so in A by the scan: «এতেষাং সাবধিকঘাতস্থানমাহ») — meaning unclear; understood as sāvadhika ("with measure").

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said]:
For [the stroke] called druta the height is said to be four fingers.*
("Uchchhrita" means "high.")
Laghu is declared to be of eight fingers, guru is of sixteen fingers,
and pluta of three times eight fingers; and druta is a slight movement of the hand.*
notes: A (by the scan) reads «দ্রুতাশ্রয়স্তু কথিতং চতুরঙ্গুলমুচ্ছ্রিতং» (drutāśrayas tu, "for druta, however"); translated by the sense ("for the one called druta").
The 1960 edition reads "চানুদ্রুতঃ" ("and anudruta"), which agrees with the beginning of the verse, where druta is of four fingers.

verses_en.text:
Now [it is told] of the ways of marking them:
Tala is marked in two ways: with sound and without sound;
in guru, pluta and the rest a soundless [stroke] is needed.*
notes: A sounded (saśabda) stroke is a clap; a soundless (niḥśabda) one is a movement of the hand without sound.

verses_en.text:
Tala: in guru, one sounded, one soundless;
in pluta, one sounded, two soundless; in anudruta,*
notes: The 1960 edition reads: "in pluta, one sounded, six soundless in it" ("ছয়" instead of "দ্বয়"); the Sanskrit verse 2991 confirms two soundless strokes.

verses_en.text:
laghu and druta the tala is without soundless [strokes].
With a loud stroke of the hand the tala is called sounded.

Thus [it is said]:
The marking of tala is twofold: with sound and without sound.
A loud stroke is sounded; laghu has only one [stroke].

For guru a double stroke is declared: one is sound, the other soundless;
and [the stroke] that goes to half — from half the sound of laghu — [is called] druta.*
notes: The meaning of the second line is unclear; translated from the reading "সোঽপ্যর্ধং যাতি চ লঘোরর্ধনাদাদ্ দ্রুত ইতি".

verses_en.text:
In pluta there is one sounded stroke, then two strokes;
they are soundless: one [is made] upward, and the other downward.

To the varieties of tala there is no end;
in the Sri rasa-mandala they all became embodied.

Krishna, joining both hands in a sweet curve,
keeps the tala thus — with what can it be compared?

Sri Radhika, displaying a wondrous grace,
joins hand to hand, smiling slightly.

The wonder that arises in the blending of the sounds
of the strokes of the hands, the bracelets and the rest — who will describe it?

Strokes of the hands in many ways, many talas in the songs —
Lakshmi and the others are amazed: with what can it be compared?

All of Radhika's companions are wonderful:
one in one tala, another in another, reveals songs.

Singing in chhayalaga is extremely difficult;
the lovely Lalita joyfully reveals it.

Krishna, supremely fond of play, to Lalita and the others
gave leave to sing kshudra songs.

Now [it is told] of kshudra song:
Mere words joined with tala and dhatu are kshudra song;
the dhatus are udgraha and the rest, described before, as is fitting.

Thus [it is said]:
Mere words joined with tala and dhatu are called kshudra.

A kshudra song is for the most part like shuddha and salaga;
consonance at the ends [of the lines] in it the shastras call praiseworthy.

The kinds of kshudra song are four: chitrapada, and also
chitrakala, dhruvapada, panchali — [so] it is known.*
notes: Chitrapada, chitrakala, dhruvapada and panchali are the four kinds of kshudra song (the third kind of nibaddha, see 2840–2845); the characteristics of the first two are given in 3005–3008.

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said]:
It is indeed fourfold: among them chitrapada is the first,
[then] chitrakala, dhruvapada and panchali — by their distinctions.

The characteristics of these songs are very extensive.
By the variety of its padas the [song] called chitrapada is known.*
notes: All copies read চিত্রকলাখ্যা ("called chitrakala"); from verse 3006 and its closing "Such is chitrapada" chitrapada is meant, while chitrakala is described in 3007–3008; translated by the sense.

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said]:
Where variety is seen in the padas alone,
and there is no variety in dhatu and the rest, know that as chitrapada.
(Variety of padas, moreover, is the possession of qualities: gentle consonance, clarity and the rest.)
Such is chitrapada.

Now, chitrakala:
Chitrakala: in the dhruva the matras are fewer, in the other [parts] equal;
from three to eight lines — such is the rule of this song.*
notes: Line — pāda, a quarter of a verse (not the pada words of 3005–3006). Matra is a unit of duration.

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said]:
If in the udgraha and abhoga the matras are equal, but in the dhruva fewer,
[and the song] is rich in lines — from three up to eight — know: that is chitrakala.

The characteristics of dhruvapada and the rest are known everywhere.
In the vernacular and in Sanskrit they sing many kinds of songs.

Songs in Sanskrit, in the vernacular and others are well known;
the knowers of sangita define [their] kinds: divya and the rest.*
notes: The vernacular (bhāṣā) is a common (non-Sanskrit) language. Divya ("divine") is a song in Sanskrit, manusha ("human") one in Prakrit or a regional language, divya-manusha one in a mixed language (3011–3012).

verses_en.text:
This is said:
Song is divya, manusha, and also divya-manusha.
Divya is composed in Sanskrit, manusha arises from Prakrit;

that arising from Sanskrit and Prakrit is called divya-manusha.
And some consider as manusha [a song] in a language that arose in a particular country.

Anga, Vanga, Kalinga and other [countries] are the sources of regional languages and the rest.
In whatever countries whatever languages are cherished,
those, taken from the speech of the people there, one should employ [in song].*
notes: Anga, Vanga and Kalinga are ancient countries of eastern India (Anga — the east of present-day Bihar, Vanga — Bengal, Kalinga — Orissa).

verses_en.text:
Some define the particulars of the composition of song and the rest:
three varieties, named sama, ardhasama and vishama.*
notes: Sama ("equal"), ardhasama ("half-equal"), vishama ("unequal") — by the number of matras in the lines (3015–3017).

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said] in Kohala:
Song is threefold: sama, ardhasama and vishama.
With four lines of equal number of matras [it] is called sama.

The song whose first and third lines are equal, and the second and fourth equal too,
is named ardhasama.

If all four lines of [a song] differ in their number of matras,
that song the sages Bharata and the others call vishama.

What further particulars there are in song — what do others know of that?
In the pastimes of the Sri rasa Krishna reveals everything.

At the singing of the sakhis Krishna, rejoicing at heart,
praising [them] much, embraces the sakhis.

From the embrace of the sakhis comes Radhika's great happiness.
What do others know of the delight that grows in song?

What can be said — the qualities of song are of many kinds,
all those that shine in the Sri rasa-mandala.

Now, the qualities of song:
The qualities of song the knowers of song have proclaimed:
graha, laya, yati, variety of mana,*
notes: Graha ("seizing") is the entry of the tala relative to the beginning of the song (3029–3037); laya is tempo (3038–3042); yati is the order in which the tempo is carried (3043–3046); mana is the concluding action of the tala (3047–3051).

verses_en.text:
repetition of dhatu, and also newness,
manifold meaning of the matu words, pleasingness of the raga,

gamaka, clarity of meaning, the charming
combination of tenna, patha and svara in various ways.

Know: these are the qualities of song — graha and the rest, nine;
in this there are further varieties of many kinds.*
notes: নয় means "nine" or possibly a negation ("not [only]"); eleven qualities are listed in 3022–3024 and 3026; the sense is unclear.

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said]:
Now the qualities of song: graha, laya and yati, variety of mana;
repetition of dhatu and newness, manifold meaning
of matu, pleasingness of the raga, then gamaka, clarity of meaning,
and the combination of tennas, svara and patha in various ways.

Moreover:
Of all these qualities the most necessary is this:
the inclusion of speech possessed of excellences, ornaments and rasa.

Graha and the rest — all the qualities that [here] are defined —
the wise expound in many ways.

Among them, on graha:
Graha is anagata, sama, atita — these three;
anagata graha and the rest — such are the three names.*
notes: Anagata ("not yet come"), sama ("simultaneous"), atita ("past").

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said]:
Tala makes the course of song even; its grahas are three,
named anagata, sama and atita — so it is held everywhere.

On anagata:
When the tala is taken before the beginning of the song,
all call this the anagata graha.

Thus [it is said]:
When before the beginning of the song two syllables are uttered
[and then] the tala is set, this is called anagata graha.
(The meaning here is this: the syllable taken in excess at the beginning of the song is "anagata": it never enters within the tala.)

On sama:
If tala and song arise at the same time,
then the wise call it the sama graha.

Thus [it is said]:
When the tala coincides [with the song] from the very utterance of the song,
then, because they arise at one time, this is called sama graha.

So also the atita graha; its kinds are many:
the knowers of sangita have set [them] forth in various ways.

Thus [it is said]:
If the kala that will fall later is placed at the beginning
and [thus] the tala is sung, then this is called tala graha.*
notes: All copies (A by the scan: «বিন্যস্য গীয়তে তালস্তদা তালগ্রহঃ স্মৃতঃ») read তালগ্রহঃ (tālagrahaḥ, "tala graha"); from the sense (the definition of atita graha) one would expect tadātītagrahaḥ ("then — atita graha"). Kala is a beat (unit of time) of the tala.

verses_en.text:
Now, laya:
Laya — [when] the evenness of the actions of graha and the rest is manifest;
it has three kinds: druta, vilambita, madhya.*
notes: The last word of the first line is, by the scan of A, apparently «স্ফুরিতে» (sphurite, "is manifest"; the OCR copies have স্থরিতে, হরিতে, C স্রিতে). Druta ("fast"), vilambita ("slow"), madhya ("middle") are the kinds of tempo.

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said]:
The mutual evenness of the actions — of song, instruments and the placing of steps —
or else [the evenness] of action and tala: this the wise call laya.
So [says] Vachaspati.*
notes: Vachaspati is a theorist of music whom Narahari quotes; his treatise is not named.

verses_en.text:
Harinayaka, however, [says]: "The pause between actions is called laya."
The wise have called it threefold: druta, madhya and vilambita.

Druta is of one matra; madhya has a pause twice [that of] druta;
vilambita is double [madhya]; all of these belong to all the talas.

Some by this define tala;
but in all views laya is a particular form of singing.

On yati:
The rule for carrying the laya is yati;
its three kinds: srotovaha, sama, gopuchchhika.*
notes: Yati here is a quality of song, the order in which the laya (tempo) is carried, not the name of a tala as in 2881. Srotovaha ("flowing as a stream"), sama ("even"), gopuchchhika ("[like] a cow's tail").

verses_en.text:
In these three particular [kinds] of pause are defined;
this the wise expound in many ways.

Thus [it is said]:
Yati is indeed the rule for carrying the laya;
it is threefold: srotovaha, sama and gopuchchhika.

Srotovaha, sama, gopuchchhika — the three [kinds] of laya;
[their] characteristics are easy; know: the shastras expound [them].

On mana:
The action of the tala that gives a pause is called mana;
one avarta bears the name vardhamana,

the second avarta is hiyamana — [so] it is determined;
the characteristics of these two, know, are known [as] easy.*
notes: Avarta is a cycle (round) of the tala; vardhamana ("increasing"), hiyamana ("decreasing"). In A (by the scan: «দ্বিতীয় আবর্ত্ত বর্দ্ধমানাখ্য নির্দ্ধার») and B, 3048 has vardhamana, as in 3047; translated after the 1960 edition and verse 3051 — hiyamana.

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said]:
The action of the tala that gives a pause is here called mana;
since it gives the tala a pause, mana completes the tala.

If it falls on the second kala in the dhruva, then
the avarta in the tala is called vardhamana — so the knowers of tala hold.

But if the mana falls on the last kala in the dhruva, then
the avarta is called hiyamana — so the wise have said.

Now, repetition of dhatu:
The way of repetition of dhatu the worthy describe:
the parts of the song are sung again and again — anew.

Manifold meaning of the matu words:
The manifold meaning of the matu words they define thus:
in a turn of speech of one [and the same] sense [words] are not used.

The characteristics of dhatu and matu [I] have made known before;
since [it is] easy, there was no detailed account.

On the pleasingness of the raga:
The evident pleasingness of the raga destroys many sorrows;
the knowers of raga reveal [its] qualities: being pleasant to the ear and the rest.

Thus [it is said]:
Pleasant to the ear, abiding in yati, with angas, bringing happiness,
rich in [the registers] mandra, madhya and tara — [such is] the desired pleasingness of a raga.

On gamaka:
The nature of gamaka is the vibration of a svara;
in the hearts of the listeners it gives rise to great happiness.

The kinds of gamaka are fifteen;
the characteristics of all, in order, beginning with tiripa, are set forth.

Thus [it is said]:
The vibration of a svara, bringing happiness to the listener's heart, is gamaka.
Its varieties are tiripa, sphurita, and also kampita,

nila, andolita, vali, tribhinna, kuvala, ahata,
unnamita, plavita, hunkrita, and also mudrita,
namita and mishrita — thus fifteen are named.*
notes: The names of the gamakas are given as in the text; in other treatises several of them are known in the forms lina (nila), kurula (kuvala), ullasita (unnamita).

verses_en.text:
Now [it is told] of their characteristics:
Lovely in its imitation of the lightest vibration of the sound of the damaru,
with a speed of a quarter of a druta — [the gamaka] is called tiripa.*
notes: The damaru is a small hourglass-shaped drum. Druta and laghu are measures of duration in the tala (a laghu is twice as long as a druta).

verses_en.text:
With a speed made of a third of a druta, [the gamaka] is held to be sphurita;
with singing at half the measure of a druta, [the gamaka] is called kampita.

Nila is with the speed of a druta, andolita with the speed of a laghu;
vali is joined with various curves — as the raga [requires].

Tribhinna is a dense sound without pauses in the three registers;
kuvala is that same vali, knotted, soft to the throat.

Ahata is when, striking the svara ahead, one turns back;
unnamita is said to be that which to svaras higher and higher

passes in order; plavita is a vibration in prolonged singing;
hunkrita is held to be [the gamaka] filled with a charming sound "hum."*
notes: Prolonged singing — pluta, an overlong sound.

verses_en.text:
Mudrita is the gamaka born of closed lips;
namita — so the knowers of sound call [the gamaka] from the lowering of the svaras.

From the mixing of these comes mishrita; it has numerous varieties;
I have not named them, since they are unfit for use and unknowable.

The way of practising this:
At night in the months of Magha and Pausha, only in the last watch,
standing in water, the practitioner should master these gamakas.*
notes: Magha and Pausha are winter months (December to February).

verses_en.text:
These are the fifteen kinds of gamaka;
some, by the distinction of the seven svaras, name seven kinds.*
notes: Couplets 3069a–3069b are not in the 1960 edition; they are in the 1912/13 edition (A, B).

verses_en.text:
Thus [it is said]:
The vibration of a svara is gamaka; by the distinction of the svaras it is sevenfold.
(The meaning is this: by the distinction of the seven svaras there are seven kinds. This, moreover, is seen in the Narada-samhita.)

Now, clarity of meaning:
When on utterance all in the words is understood,
a faultless meaning full of rasa is called clarity.

Thus [it is said]:
When on the utterance of speech the meaning is fully grasped,
[and] the meaning is pleasant, faultless and with rasa — that indeed is clarity of meaning.

The placing of tena, patha and svara with variety:
tena is used after patha and svara, and never at the beginning.

What fault arises in song from the absence of the qualities and the rest —
of that know something; this the knowers of song expound at length.

Without tala — illness, without dhatu — loss of wealth;
a song without dhatu, matu and pada is an enemy.

Thus [it is said]:
Without tala — illness of the body, without dhatu — loss of wealth;
where there are no dhatu, matu and pada, that song is an enemy.

Now [it is told] of the faults of song:
Some say the faults of song are of many kinds;
others define [them] briefly: stumbling of speech and the rest.

Thus [it is said]:
The faults in songs are: stumbling of speech and the rest,
composition lacking tala and the rest,
impairment of dhatu, matu and the rest, harsh words,
loss of rasa and the rest, unpleasantness to the ear.

Although in songs there are many such and similar faults,
they are not named [here]; if [one needs] to grasp them in knowledge, let one look into this and that [in the books].*
notes: So in A (by the scan: «নোক্তাস্তে চেদ্গ্রহস্তেষাং জ্ঞানে তত্ত্বিলোক্যতাং») and B: জ্ঞানে (jñāne, "in knowledge"); the 1960 edition has গানে ("if they appear in singing, let them be noticed").

verses_en.text:
One who sings a song is called a singer;
the characteristics of a singer are set forth in various ways.

[It is told] of the characteristics of a singer:
Singers are of three kinds: the best, the middling, the lowest;
the characteristics of these three the shastras set forth plainly.

Thus [it is said]:
A singer is said to be of three kinds: the best, the middling, the lowest.
With a pure-sounding voice, with a good sharira, knowing the distinctions of many ragas,*
notes: Sharira (śārīra) in music theory is the natural quality of the voice, the capacity to manifest a raga without training; the 1960 edition understands suśārīra as "with a handsome body."

verses_en.text:
endowed with graha, mana and laya, knowing tala, having conquered fatigue,
with easy and graceful movement in gamakas touching the three sthanas,*
notes: Graha (here the point at which the song enters relative to the tala), mana (measure) and laya (tempo) are terms of the theory of tala. The sthanas are the three registers of the voice.

verses_en.text:
skilled in singing prabandhas, intent on careful performance,
master of his voice, knowing the sthayi, faultless, endowed with [good] retention —

[such is] the best. The middling is named [one endowed] with some of these qualities;
but one who, though endowed with qualities, is full of faults is called the lowest.

There is also [a division] into five kinds — shikshakara and the rest:
one skilled in teaching [is called] a shikshakara; thus are known the shikshakara and the others.

Thus [it is said]:
Shikshakara, anukara, rasika, and also ranjaka
and bhavaka — thus the knowers of song have called the singer fivefold.

One skilled in teaching without omission is held by the virtuous to be a shikshakara;
one who imitates the manner of others is called an anukara.

One absorbed in rasa is a rasika; one who delights the listeners is a ranjaka;
one who imparts a special excellence to the song is called a bhavaka.

The wise further speak of singers of three kinds:
one, two, many — these are the plain characteristics.

Thus [it is said]:
The singer is of three kinds: ekala, yamala and vrinda.
One who sings entirely alone is an ekala singer;
one who has a second is a yamala; one who is with a group is a vrinda singer.

[It is told] of the faults of a singer:
The faults of a singer are of many kinds:
timidity, indistinct words and the rest are well known in the shastras.

Thus [it is said]:
Timid, with indistinct words, shaking his head, puffing, off-key,
with clenched teeth, closing his eyes, and also unsteady in the grama,
singing with a twisted neck, [now] scanty, [now] excessive in svaras, mixing ragas,
with trembling body, inattentive, making [the song] insipid, crow-voiced, hasty.
("Crow" means with a harsh cry.)

Moreover:
falling out of tala, stretching the body of the song, frightful in appearance, goat-throated, unsteady,
